* ENH: Cumulative Numba GPU changes (#2523)

* Trigger CI on PRs to this branch

* ENH: support array-API (GPU-resident) buffers in DistanceMatrix (#2499)

* ENH: support array-API buffers in DistanceMatrix

Allow DistanceMatrix to hold a non-NumPy array-API buffer (e.g. a GPU-resident cupy/torch/jax array) instead of coercing it to NumPy at construction. Validation, permute, copy and filter dispatch to an array-API path for non-NumPy buffers; the NumPy path is unchanged. Adds array-API tests for DistanceMatrix.

* MAINT: move DistanceMatrix array-API handling into shared helpers

Move the non-NumPy (array-API) branches out of the DistanceMatrix and
SymmetricMatrix methods into the helpers they already call, so the class
methods no longer special-case the buffer type. is_symmetric_and_hollow,
distmat_reorder and distmat_reorder_condensed now handle a non-NumPy
buffer directly, and a new copy_array helper in skbio.util._array copies
a buffer on its own device. _validate_data, _validate_shape, permute,
filter and copy just call these.

Also align the non-NumPy path with the NumPy one: a non-floating buffer
is cast to float64 (float32/float64 are kept), and _validate_shape
accepts the same single/double precision dtypes on both paths. Non-NumPy
buffers are stored in redundant (2-D) form only; a condensed or 1-D
non-NumPy buffer is rejected rather than silently copied to the host,
since condensed storage relies on scipy.squareform.

* MAINT: restore original _validate_data control flow

The array-API handling now lives in the is_symmetric and
is_symmetric_and_hollow helpers, so _validate_data keeps its original form.

* ENH: support condensed form for GPU-resident distance matrices (#2505)

* ENH: support condensed form for GPU-resident distance matrices

Extend the array-API (GPU-resident) DistanceMatrix support so the condensed-form conversions work on a non-NumPy buffer, and so the host-side export helpers no longer assume NumPy. condensed_form on a non-NumPy 2-D buffer now extracts the row-major upper triangle on-device via the existing distmat_reorder_condensed helper instead of calling scipy.squareform, and a non-NumPy buffer can be constructed in condensed form or expanded back to redundant form. plot and to_data_frame materialize the matrix to the host before handing it to matplotlib and pandas, which are host-only. Adds array-API tests for both matrix classes across the condensed round-trip, the host-side exports, and a non-zero diagonal.

* ENH: array-API (GPU-resident) support for permanova and mantel (#2503)

* ENH: array-API (GPU-resident) support for permanova and mantel

Dispatch permanova and mantel on where the DistanceMatrix data lives: a NumPy-backed DM keeps the existing cython/numba engine path unchanged, while a non-NumPy (e.g. GPU-resident cupy/torch/jax) buffer is computed through the array-API (xp) namespace so the matrix stays on its device. For mantel this covers pearson and spearman; kendalltau has no xp path and is materialized on the host. IDs are aligned exactly like the NumPy path (reorder, strict, lookup), and the permutation p-values match the NumPy path to floating-point precision. Adds array-API tests for both functions.

* ENH: Mantel warns and falls back to the NumPy path on mixed-backend inputs

* TEST: cover permanova and Mantel array-API helpers under NumPy CI

* MAINT: run the Array API CI on PRs to the development branch

* BUG: validate distance matrices backed by a read-only array

is_symmetric_and_hollow copied the input only when it was not C-contiguous, so a read-only but contiguous buffer (for example a NumPy array shared from an immutable JAX array via __dlpack__) reached the Cython kernel and tripped its writable typed memoryview with "buffer source array is read-only". Copy whenever the buffer is not both C-contiguous and writable, so any array-API backend that materializes to a read-only NumPy array validates correctly.

* MAINT: use _get_array instead of the test-only _to_numpy in mantel

_to_numpy is documented for test assertions rather than library functions; _get_array is the library-facing conversion and attempts a zero-copy __dlpack__ view before falling back.

* BUG: store a writable buffer for a distance matrix built from a read-only array

The earlier copy in is_symmetric_and_hollow only let validation pass; the matrix still stored the read-only buffer, so permute/reorder later failed in distmat_reorder_condensed_cy with "buffer source array is read-only". Copy once in DistanceMatrix.__init__ when the input is a read-only or non-C-contiguous NumPy array, so validation, permutation and reordering all read a writable buffer, and revert the now-redundant is_symmetric_and_hollow change. Writable inputs stay zero-copy and non-NumPy buffers are left on their device.

* BUG: accumulate permanova s_T in float64 for float32 distance matrices (#2509)

* BUG: accumulate permanova s_T in float64 for float32 distance matrices

The total sum of squares s_T was accumulated in the matrix dtype. For a float32 distance matrix this loses accuracy in the pseudo-F: s_T and the within-group sum of squares s_W nearly cancel in s_A = s_T - s_W, so a small float32 rounding error in s_T is amplified in the ratio. On real float32 UniFrac matrices this reached several percent at large sizes (about 5% at 25k). s_W was already accumulated in double; accumulating s_T in float64 too makes the two consistent, in both the DistanceMatrix (Cython/Numba) path and the array-API path. Float64 matrices are unaffected.

* DOC: add CHANGELOG entry for the permanova float32 s_T fix

* ENH: add optional Numba engine for center_distance_matrix (#2508)

* ENH: add optional Numba engine for center_distance_matrix

Adds a Numba implementation of distance-matrix double-centering, selectable through engine="numba" on center_distance_matrix and pcoa alongside the existing Cython path. The Numba kernels mirror the Cython implementation in _cutils.pyx (e_matrix_means_cy and f_matrix_inplace_cy), including the 24-wide block tiling, so the two engines are numerically interchangeable. Numba stays an optional dependency with Cython as the default, extending the engine= selector already used by permanova and mantel to the ordination centering step.

* DOC: add CHANGELOG entry for the center_distance_matrix Numba engine

* Known issue: Engine not honored by SKBB.

* MAINT: skip the scikit-bio-binaries path when engine="numba" in permanova and pcoa (#2510)

* MAINT: skip the scikit-bio-binaries path when engine="numba"

When engine="numba" is requested, permanova and pcoa (method="fsvd") no longer take the scikit-bio-binaries path. That path is the Cython-equivalent acceleration, so entering it contradicts a numba request. The binaries availability is gated on the resolved engine, skipped for "numba" and kept for "cython" and the default. pcoa now resolves the engine once at the top, like permanova already does, so pcoa(engine="numba") requires Numba to be installed even for a GPU-resident matrix, matching permanova.

* DOC: add CHANGELOG entry for the engine="numba" binaries gate


* MAINT: simplify the pcoa binaries gate to a direct engine check

Drop the early _resolve_engine call and check engine != "numba" at the
availability test itself. This is enough to skip the scikit-bio-binaries
fsvd path when Numba is requested, and it avoids the extra ImportError a
top-level resolve would raise for a GPU-resident matrix that never needs
Numba installed.

* ENH: add a Numba GPU backend for permanova and mantel (#2511)

* ENH: add a Numba GPU backend for permanova and mantel

Add a fused single-source Numba kernel for the permanova and mantel permutation tests, compiled through numba.cuda on NVIDIA and numba.hip on AMD. When engine="numba" and the DistanceMatrix is already on a GPU device, the kernel runs on the device-resident matrix in place; if it cannot build or run on the current stack the call warns once and falls back to the array-API path, which is correct on any backend. Permutations are drawn on the host in the same RNG order as the other engines, so p-values match cython, numba and xp exactly.

* DOC: add CHANGELOG entries for the permanova/mantel Numba GPU backend

* DOC: scope the GPU speedup claim to a datacenter GPU and clarify a comment

The CHANGELOG entry said the fused kernel is "much faster than the CPU
engines" without qualification, but on an entry-level GPU the permanova
gain over the CPU Numba engine is modest; the large speedup is on a
datacenter GPU, so the claim is scoped to that. Also reword the CuPy
routing note in _gpu.py to state the reason (different GPU vendors)
rather than an untested crash.

* PERF: keep the GPU kernels' per-element math in the matrix dtype

Both fused kernels upcast each matrix element to float64 before the
per-element multiply. The input is already float32 and the sum is
accumulated in float64 regardless, so the upcast adds no accuracy and,
on consumer GPUs with weak fp64, dominates the runtime. Compute the
per-element products in the matrix dtype and keep only the accumulator
in float64. On an RTX 4060 this cuts the permanova kernel from about
10.8 s to 5.7 s at 25000 samples with 999 permutations; it is a no-op
for float64 input and speed-neutral on the MI300X.

* ENH: run the fused GPU kernel on ROCm CuPy buffers

_numba_gpu_module_for sent every CuPy array to numba.cuda, so a CuPy
array on an AMD GPU fell back to the array-API path instead of the fused
kernel. CuPy reports the same array-API namespace for its CUDA and ROCm
builds; use the build's own is_hip flag to route a ROCm CuPy buffer to
numba.hip, mirroring the torch branch's use of torch.version.hip. The
kernel then runs on AMD CuPy matrices (verified on an MI300X, permanova
and mantel matching the cython reference); the torch path is unchanged
and the warn-once fallback still covers any stack where the kernel
cannot build.

Also drop the mock-based routing unit test: it stubbed the very APIs it
checked (is_hip, sys.modules), so it verified only branch wiring; the
routing is trivial, validated on hardware, and exercised by the
gpu-gated dispatch tests.

* TEST: drop mock from the GPU dispatch tests

The permanova and mantel fallback tests patched the dispatch internals
(is_numpy_array, _numba_gpu_module_for, _run_*_gpu, _mark_gpu_unavailable)
to simulate a kernel failure, which can only happen with a GPU present.
They verified wiring rather than behavior and cannot run in CI without a
GPU. Drop them; the kernel is validated on hardware. Rewrite the warn-once
test to use a real NumPy array instead of patching the backend lookup, so
no test relies on mock.

* ENH: make the DM class family fully device-resident (#2515)

* ENH: make the DM class family fully device-resident

Two spots still forced a non-NumPy (e.g. GPU-resident) buffer to the host:

- distmat_reorder_condensed_py, used by filter() and permute() when a
  matrix is stored condensed, always converted its input to a NumPy
  array. The reorder indices are cheap to compute on the host; only the
  actual gather now runs on the input's device, matching the pattern
  already used by distmat_reorder and distmat_reorder_condensed.

- PairwiseMatrix (the asymmetric DissimilarityMatrix base) could not
  hold a non-NumPy buffer at all: its input normalization asserted a
  NumPy array, its shape validation compared dtypes against
  np.float32/np.float64 directly (which never matches a non-NumPy
  dtype object), and its copy path called data.copy(), which not every
  backend implements. All three now mirror the patterns already used by
  SymmetricMatrix: ingest_array to preserve the buffer and its device,
  xp.isdtype for the dtype check, and copy_array for a backend-safe
  copy. A 1D condensed vector on a non-NumPy backend, which cannot be
  symmetric-expanded by scipy's squareform, is expanded via a single
  host round-trip and placed back on the input's device rather than
  raising.

Verified on both an AMD MI300X (torch-ROCm) and an NVIDIA RTX 4060
(CuPy): condensed-form filter and permute stay on-device and match the
NumPy reference, and a DissimilarityMatrix built from a device buffer
stays on-device through construction, copy, and transpose.

Added array-backend tests (numpy, jax, torch, cupy) for both: filter
and permute on a condensed-stored DistanceMatrix, and a new
PairwiseMatrixArrayAPITests class covering construction, dtype
casting, copy, transpose, and the 1D condensed input case for the
asymmetric matrix.

* ENH: scatter the 1D condensed input on-device for torch and cupy

Igor asked whether the host round-trip for a 1D condensed vector on a
non-NumPy backend could be avoided. For torch and cupy, which support
item-assignment, it can: scatter the values into the upper triangle
on-device and mirror to the lower triangle, the same approach already
used by SymmetricMatrix._condensed_to_redundant for its mutable-backend
case. JAX, which does not support item-assignment, keeps the host
round-trip, matching that same method's immutable-backend fallback.

Verified on an AMD MI210 (torch-ROCm): the on-device scatter matches
the NumPy reference.

* DOC: note the possibility of a native per-backend implementation

A comment documenting that a native per-backend or Numba/GPU kernel
implementation could replace the JAX host round-trip, per Igor's review
comment.

* MAINT: consolidate condensed-to-redundant expansion into one function

_condensed_to_redundant duplicated the same numpy/torch/cupy/jax logic
that PairwiseMatrix.__init__ implemented separately for its own 1D
input handling, and excluded JAX from the on-device scatter entirely
(it fell back to a host round-trip through squareform).

Pull the expansion logic into a single _expand_condensed(condensed,
diagonal=None) function defined ahead of PairwiseMatrix, so the
constructor can call it directly instead of duplicating the branch.
It handles numpy and array-API buffers in one place instead of
branching at each call site, extends the on-device scatter to JAX via
its functional .at[].set() update (mutable backends still use
item-assignment), and reuses the existing _vec_to_shape helper instead
of re-deriving n from k inline.

_condensed_to_redundant is removed, no remaining callers.

Verified against numpy, torch, and jax backends (185 passed each), and
against the diagonal-preserving redundant_form() path specifically
since that method's behavior depends on this function directly.

* BUG: fix center_distance_matrix public wiring and two torch pcoa crashes (#2520)

The public skbio.stats.ordination.center_distance_matrix was wired to the wrong function. __init__.py imported it from _utils.py, a NumPy-only implementation used internally by pcoa() as its Cython/Numba-accelerated engine, instead of from _principal_coordinate_analysis.py, where the actual array-API-aware version already lives and which pcoa() itself correctly calls. A user calling the public name on a torch, jax, or cupy buffer would hit the NumPy-only path and crash. Fixed the import to point at the right function. This changes nothing for NumPy input, since the array-API-aware version still calls the same Cython/Numba engine for a real np.ndarray.

pcoa() crashed on torch for both the eigh and fsvd methods. xp.isclose(eigvals, 0) fails because the array-API standard requires both arguments to be arrays, and torch's backend enforces that strictly while NumPy and JAX tolerate a bare Python int. Fixed with xp.zeros_like(eigvals). Fixing that surfaced a second crash in the same block: eigvals.argsort()[::-1] also fails on torch, which does not support negative-step slicing. Fixed with xp.flip(eigvals.argsort(), axis=0).

Added versionadded 0.7.4 tags and the array-API compatibility grid to permanova, mantel, pcoa, and center_distance_matrix, with backends numpy, jax, torch, and cupy.

Verified both pcoa fixes against a NumPy reference on torch and jax, both eigh and fsvd, agreement under 4e-16. Also checked cupy specifically on AMD's cupy-ROCm build, since it is not installed locally: both fixed expressions run clean with correct values.

Added TestPCoABackends, covering both eigh and fsvd against a NumPy reference across numpy, jax, torch, and cupy, and a direct identity test guarding the wiring fix specifically, since the existing TestCenterDistanceMatrixBackends imports center_distance_matrix directly from _principal_coordinate_analysis and would never have caught the public-import bug. Neither of the two bugs had any test coverage before this.

* DOC: note the default-device requirement of the Numba GPU kernels (#2529)

The fused Numba GPU kernels for permanova and mantel allocate and launch on Numba's current device, so a GPU buffer that belongs to a different device is not supported. Nothing detects the mismatch: __cuda_array_interface__ carries no device field, the launch itself reports no error, and on ROCm the illegal access surfaces only at the next synchronizing call and leaves the GPU context unusable for the rest of the process, so a later and entirely valid operation fails instead.

Document this as a known limitation in the permanova and mantel docstrings, next to the existing ROCm-PyTorch note, and add a multi-GPU section to the array API developer page. Both state that GPU buffers must belong to the default device and that the way to use several devices is to change the default to match the buffer ownership before calling, through numba.cuda.select_device or numba.hip.select_device. The array-API path is unaffected and honors whichever device the input is on, since its allocations all take device= from the input.

Checked on an eight-GPU MI300X node: a torch buffer on a non-default device launches without error and then faults at the copy back, after which a valid same-device operation in the same process also fails, and selecting the buffer's device beforehand gives correct results. The CUDA equivalent is untested because the NVIDIA machine available has a single GPU, so the context behaviour is attributed to ROCm only.

* BUG: fix three GPU-only failures in the array-API paths (#2530)

Turning on the GPU CI job surfaced six failing tests across torch, jax and cupy. They come from three separate places, all of which only manifest on a device, which is why the CPU jobs stayed green throughout.

In `_get_array`, the fallback that converts a non-NumPy array to NumPy catches AttributeError, TypeError and RuntimeError, but `np.from_dlpack` raises BufferError for a GPU-resident buffer. The comment above that except clause already describes the CUDA case, so the fallback was meant to fire and never did. Adding BufferError to the tuple lets it work as intended; this is what the four failing mantel tests were hitting.

In `pcoa`, `xp.arange(eigvals.shape[0])` was created without a device, so on a device-resident input the mask ended up on the host while the eigenvalues were on the GPU, and the comparison against `num_positive` failed. It now takes `device=eigvals.device`.

The table constructors are the third. `_create_table` and `_create_table_1d` build pandas, NumPy or polars objects, all of which are host-side, but nothing brought a device-resident array back first: CuPy refuses the implicit conversion outright and PyTorch refuses it for a CUDA tensor. Rather than fix this inside `pcoa` alone, a `_to_host` helper now runs at the top of both constructors so every caller benefits. It is guarded to a non-NumPy array-API object, so for NumPy arrays, DataFrames and lists, which is everything the existing call sites pass, it returns immediately and nothing changes.

Verified with the CI command, `pytest -m array_api --pyargs skbio`, on an NVIDIA RTX 4060: 48 passed on each of torch, jax and cupy, against six failures before. Also 16 passed on an AMD MI300X under torch-ROCm, so both vendors. The ordination, table, IO and distance suites pass unchanged on numpy, torch and jax on CPU.

* MAINT: move the coverage configuration into pyproject.toml (#2538)

Main dropped `.coveragerc` in #2533 and moved the coverage configuration into `pyproject.toml`, so its Makefile and workflows now pass `--rcfile ../pyproject.toml`. This branch still carries the old file and still points at it, which leaves the two out of step and means anything added here that names the old file stops working once the branch reaches main, since coverage exits with an error rather than falling back when the rcfile is missing.

Mirror the same change here: drop `.coveragerc` along with its now-dead check-manifest entry, copy main's `[tool.coverage.run]` and `[tool.coverage.report]` sections into `pyproject.toml` verbatim, and repoint the Makefile, ci.yml and numba.yml. numba.yml needs no separate change to its test step, because it runs `make test` and picks the command up from the Makefile. This also brings the `**/tests/**` omit pattern from #2531, replacing the `*/tests*` form that was not matching reliably.

* MAINT: run the Numba GPU kernels in array-API CI and report coverage (#2535)

* TEST: exercise the fused Numba GPU kernels from the array-API suite

The array-API GPU job selects `-m array_api`, and no test in that selection combined a device-resident matrix with `engine="numba"`, so the fused GPU kernels in `_permanova_gpu` and `_mantel_gpu` were never executed. `array_api` and `numba` are independent markers but nothing carried both, and `pytest -m "array_api and numba"` collected nothing.

Stack `@numba_code` on `@array_backends(...)` for one permanova and one mantel test so both markers apply. `numba_code` skips when Numba is absent and `array_backends` already skips unavailable backend and device combinations, so the tests stay inert wherever they cannot run.

* MAINT: install numba-cuda in the GPU job and report array-API coverage

The GPU job had no Numba GPU support installed, so `_numba_gpu_module_for` returned None and the fused kernels were skipped in favor of the array-API fallback. Install `numba-cuda[cu12]`, matching the CUDA 12 stack already pinned for the other backends, and assert that `numba.cuda.is_available()` holds. Without the assertion a missing install leaves the job green while the kernels it covers never run.

Run both array-API jobs under `coverage` and upload to Codecov, mirroring `ci.yml`. This workflow had no coverage step, so the code it exercised was absent from the coverage report.

* TEST: cover the host-side GPU paths and exclude the device kernels

The bodies of the `@gpu.jit` kernels compile to PTX and run on the device, so CPython never executes them and coverage.py reports them as missed however well the kernel is tested. That is 56 of the 98 statements in `_permanova_gpu` and 48 of the 123 in `_mantel_gpu`, which is most of why those files looked untested. Mark both `# pragma: no cover`, as `skbio/util/_gpu.py` and `_typing.py` already do, so the measurement describes code that can actually be measured.

The rest of both modules is ordinary host-side Python. `_run_mantel_gpu` validates its inputs and handles the constant, near-constant and zero-permutation cases before it touches its `gpu` argument, so those branches run on NumPy input with no device present; the same holds for `_assemble_fp` with no permutations. Add those to the existing host-side test classes, and add device-resident tests for the `alternative` variants and the float32 path, which are only reachable once the kernel has produced real output.

* BUG: keep the mantel fallback reproducible when the GPU kernel fails (#2537)

`mantel()` builds one generator with `get_rng(seed)` and hands the same object to `_run_mantel_gpu` and, when that raises, to `_mantel_stats_pearson_xp`. The kernel path draws its permutations in `_perm_order` before the launch that can fail, so by the time the fallback runs the generator has already been advanced and the fallback draws a different permutation set. The same seed then produces a different p-value depending on whether the kernel happened to work, which the array-API GPU job hit on a runner where the kernel cannot launch.

Pass `seed` rather than a live generator and let each callee derive its own, as `_run_permanova_gpu` already does. `_run_mantel_gpu` and `_mantel_stats_pearson_xp` both take `seed` now, and the two NumPy-path calls pass it as well; those two already declared `seed` but were being handed the generator. Nothing receives the caller's generator any more, so a failed attempt cannot consume it. For a seeded run each path draws the same permutations as before, so a successful launch is unaffected.

The kendalltau path is the exception and keeps its own generator: it permutes inside the loop, so it needs one that advances between iterations rather than a seed that would repeat the same draw.

The one test that calls `_mantel_stats_pearson_xp` with permutations now passes the seed directly rather than a generator, matching the new signature.

* Preserve non-zero diagonal in SymmetricMatrix.filter/permute on condensed matrices (#2536)

SymmetricMatrix.filter() and .permute() reconstruct their result from the
condensed form via self.__class__(..., condensed=True) without passing
diagonal=. The condensed representation stores only off-diagonal values, so the
constructor defaults the diagonal to 0, silently resetting a SymmetricMatrix's
non-zero diagonal. DistanceMatrix never surfaces this because it is always
hollow, and the failure is silent because __eq__ compares only off-diagonal
data.

Introduce an overridable _diagonal_kwargs(idxs=None) helper: PairwiseMatrix
returns {}, SymmetricMatrix threads the diagonal (subsetting/reordering an array
diagonal by idxs, passing a scalar diagonal through unchanged), and
DistanceMatrix overrides back to {} (it stays hollow and its constructor does
not accept diagonal=). The helper is threaded through the three condensed
reconstruction sites (filter same-ids fast path, filter subset, permute).

Fixes #2516.

* BUG: pass permdisp's seed down to pcoa (#2546)

* BUG: pass permdisp's seed down to pcoa

permdisp accepts a seed and its docstring states that the seed makes the output deterministic, but it calls pcoa without forwarding it. The eigh solver is deterministic so this goes unnoticed there, while fsvd draws a random projection from an unseeded generator, so a seeded permdisp call using method="fsvd" returns a different ordination, and therefore a different statistic and p-value, on every invocation. On a 60 by 60 matrix repeated calls with the same seed disagree in every run; on larger inputs the p-value can move far enough to change the conclusion.

Forward the seed. The eigh path does not consume it, so results there are unchanged; only the fsvd path is affected, and it had no reproducible behavior to preserve.

The existing fsvd tests do not catch this because their distance matrix is nine by nine, small enough that every random projection recovers the same subspace. The regression test uses a matrix large enough for the projections to disagree, and no permutations, since the observed statistic alone depends on the ordination.

* ENH: add a Numba engine for permdisp (#2547)

* ENH: add a Numba engine for permdisp

permdisp gains engine="numba", resolved through _resolve_engine the same way permanova and mantel do. The Cython path is untouched and stays the default.

The Numba path batches the permutation loop rather than evaluating one grouping at a time. Each replicate is only O(n * d) work with d the retained ordination dimensions, so the parallel axis is the permutation itself and the per-call overhead of the sequential Monte Carlo loop is what dominates at the default ten dimensions. Groupings are generated in chunks of 32 per thread, which keeps every worker supplied and bounds the grouping buffer to CHUNK x n instead of letting it grow with the permutation count.

test="median" needs the geometric median, so geomedian_axis_one is ported alongside the F statistic; without it the engine argument would be a no-op for the default test. The port keeps the same modified Weiszfeld iteration and the same convergence test as the Cython original, and agrees with it to 1e-12 or better across a few hundred random shapes. It differs in one place, deliberately: the test for every sample coinciding with the running estimate runs before the weights are normalized rather than after, because the Cython divides by a zero weight total on that input and raises before reaching its own test for it.

The kernels compute the one-way ANOVA inline instead of calling scipy.stats.f_oneway, which the Cython path uses. The two agree to about 4e-15 relative on the statistic at a hundred samples and 2e-13 at five thousand, and return the same inf and nan in the degenerate cases where the within-group term vanishes. Permutations are drawn in the same order as _run_monte_carlo_stats, so p-values are unchanged.

* DOC: add changelog link for the permdisp Numba engine

* TEST: limit the tied-statistic check to the centroid test

The six sample fixture in this test exists to manufacture exact ties, so that a permutation statistic equal to the observed one distinguishes the ">=" the p-value uses from a ">". It compared both center definitions, and the median half fails on x86-64 while passing on arm64.

The cause is on the Cython side and predates this work. _compute_groups builds its group list in np.unique label order and passes it to scipy.stats.f_oneway, so relabeling swaps the arguments, and f_oneway is not invariant to their order. On the median distances of this fixture that costs a last bit; on the centroid distances it happens not to. Measured on x86-64: the group centers and the per-sample distances are bit identical across the swap, and only f_oneway differs, by 1.332e-15. On the fixture 98 of 999 permutations reproduce the observed partition; the Cython median statistic matches for all 98 on arm64 but for 61 of 98 on x86-64, moving the p-value from 0.099 to 0.062. The numba kernels compute the ANOVA inline over a fixed sample order rather than calling SciPy per group, so they are order invariant and report 98 on both.

The centroid statistic reproduces exactly on both architectures in both engines, so restricting the comparison to it keeps the property the test is there for while dropping an equality that was never guaranteed. The reason is recorded in the test so the omission does not read as an oversight.

* MAINT: match cython's return type and dtype rules in the numba engine

Two places where switching engine changed something it should not.

permdisp builds its result with an object dtype Series, so the type of each entry is visible to the caller. The Cython path leaves the p-value as the NumPy scalar the arithmetic produces, while the numba driver wrapped it in float(), so the same call returned np.float64 under one engine and float under the other. permanova's numba driver already returns the scalar unwrapped; this matches both.

The docstring states that a spatial median on an ordination that is not single or double precision raises, which is what happens on the Cython path because geomedian_axis_one is a fused type function with only those two signatures. The numba driver widened whatever it was given instead, so an integer ordination returned nan and a half precision one returned a number, in both cases silently. It now rejects the same inputs the Cython path rejects. Single precision stays accepted by both; the kernel computes it in double, which leaves the statistic differing in the seventh significant figure; across the seed and test combinations I checked the p-value did not move.

Both behaviors now have tests; neither did before, and mutation testing is what showed it.

* DOC: correct three kernel docstrings that describe the earlier design

Three comments were written before the driver was chunked and before the geometric median's zero distance test was moved, and they still described the older behavior.

The batch kernel no longer evaluates the whole permutation loop in one call, it evaluates one chunk per call. The geometric median does not handle samples coinciding with the running estimate the same way as the Cython original, it deliberately tests for that case before normalizing the weights rather than after, which is the whole point of the change. And the driver does not make the p-value match the Cython engine exactly, it makes both engines see the same groupings in the same order.

Also two British spellings in comments, in a module that is otherwise US throughout.

* DOC: clarify the dtype guard comment in the permdisp Numba engine

The comment above the dtype check ended with "Match that rather than
silently widening whatever comes in", six lines above a cast that widens
float32 to float64, so it read as a claim that nothing is ever widened.

Split it in two. The check keeps a comment describing what it rejects and
why, and notes that it is not conditioned on the test, so it is stricter
than Cython for test="centroid", which never reaches geomedian_axis_one.
The cast gets its own comment saying an accepted float32 ordination is
deliberately accumulated in float64, and that Cython computes in the input
dtype instead, so the engines differ by float32 precision on such an input.

Comments only. No behavior change.

* MAINT: avoid redundant recomputation in dirmult_ttest's Welch's t-test

The closed-form parity test re-derived vn1/vn2/se/dof by copy-pasting

with a confusing TypeError from range() instead of the documented

* MAINT: reuse scratch buffers in _welch_draw_stats instead of reallocating

Every draw allocated 6 fresh length-m arrays even though the shapes
never change across draws. Rewrite to write into pre-allocated
buffers via out= and in-place ops instead: the three outputs write
directly into the caller's (draws, m) rows, and four scratch buffers

shrinks as m grows, since allocation overhead is a smaller fraction

* PERF: reuse Gamma-draw buffer, precompute variance means, transform in place

Reuses the Gamma-sampling buffer across draws in _dirmult_draw (largest
per-draw allocation, previously untouched by the earlier buffer-reuse
pass), applies the CLR log/center transform to it in place instead of
via the shared clr(), passes precomputed means into np.var via NumPy

Replaces the (draws, features) diff/se/dof arrays and their downstream
tstat/pval/lower/upper temporaries with running sums and running
min/max over (features,) buffers, updated per draw. Peak RSS drops
47% at 25k features on an isolated node (479.6MB -> 252.9MB); time is

scipy.special.stdtr/stdtrit 128 times on (features,) arrays instead of
once on the full (draws, features) array.

Summing sequentially instead of via a single (draws, features)
.mean(axis=0) can differ from the prior output at floating-point noise
level; the doctest's fixed-seed example still matches to 6 decimals.

* MAINT: cut dirmult_ttest's per-draw scratch buffers, fix row-mean reuse

Reduces the streaming loop's per-draw scratch from 9 buffers to 5:
work now holds the t-statistic, then the p-value, then the

folded into a running sum. Moves the p-value's *2.0 out of the loop

* ENH: Add NCBI genetic code tables 26-33 and fix table 3's start codons (#2563)

* ENH: Add NCBI genetic code tables 26-33 and fix table 3's start codons

NCBI's genetic code table (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Taxonomy/Utils/
wprintgc.cgi) now goes up to table 33, but scikit-bio's
`_ncbi_genetic_codes` table stopped at 25. This adds tables 26-33:
Pachysolen tannophilus Nuclear, Karyorelict Nuclear, Condylostoma
Nuclear, Mesodinium Nuclear, Peritrich Nuclear, Blastocrithidia
Nuclear, Balanophoraceae Plastid, and Cephalodiscidae Mitochondrial.

Data (`AAs`/`Starts` strings) was sourced directly from NCBI's
canonical ASN.1 table (ftp://ftp.ncbi.nih.gov/entrez/misc/data/gc.prt)
to guarantee accuracy. NCBI's `Starts` field marks some codon
positions with `*` to flag context-dependent stop/sense ambiguity in
these newer ciliate-like codes; scikit-bio's `starts` field only
models `M` (start) vs not, so these are folded into `-`, consistent
with how the existing tables already encode NCBI's stop-related `*`
markers. As a side effect, tables 27 and 28 become indistinguishable
under `GeneticCode.__eq__` (same `amino_acids` and `starts`); `test_ne`
is updated to deduplicate before asserting pairwise inequality.

Also corrected table 3 (Yeast Mitochondrial), which was missing `GTG`
as an alternative start codon -- present in NCBI's table per their
changelog ("Version 4.4: Added GTG as start codon for genetic code
3") but never synced into scikit-bio's copy.

Fixes #1659.

* BUG: apply the permdisp Numba dtype check per test (#2569)

_run_permdisp_numba rejected any ordination that was not float32 or
float64, on the grounds that the Cython path raises there. That is only
true of the median test, which reaches geomedian_axis_one, a fused
function with just those two signatures. The centroid test never
reaches that kernel and is computed with numpy, so Cython returned a
statistic for an integer ordination while the Numba engine raised
TypeError.

This also contradicted permdisp's own documented Raises section, which
scopes the restriction to the median test and names the centroid test
as the way around it. Under engine="numba" that advice did not work.

Check per test instead, so engine= selects an implementation without
changing which inputs are legal. The median test keeps the float32 or
float64 requirement. The centroid test accepts any numeric dtype and
rejects the rest, which is what numpy can and cannot do arithmetic on,
and matches where the Cython path itself raises.

On an integer ordination the two engines now agree to 1.9e-15 with
identical p-values, because numpy's mean promotes integers to float64
before the Cython path uses them.

The existing dtype test only exercised test="median", which is why this
was missed. It now covers the centroid case both ways: int64 and int32
are computed and agree across engines, and an object ordination is
refused by both.
